titel: Tulip mania, the Mississippi Bubble and the South Sea Bubble
kurz: Three speculative manias between 1637 and 1720 and the credit mechanism that all three had in common.

bloecke.md:
On 5 February 1637, an orphanage in the Dutch town of Alkmaar auctioned off the bulb collection of a deceased innkeeper. The auction raised around 90,000 guilders. At the time, a craftsman earned about 150 guilders a year, and up to 300 in well-paid trades.

Two days earlier, at a tavern auction in Haarlem, not a single bulb had found a buyer. No new piece of news, no crop failure and no decree preceded the collapse. All that was missing was the next buyer. Markets whose price rests solely on the expectation of further buyers collapse in this way without any external trigger.

bloecke.titel: Price of a Semper Augustus bulb in years of a craftsman's income
bloecke.unter: Calculated with an annual income of 150 guilders; for 1637, a price of 30,000 guilders for three bulbs is recorded. The individual prices come from contemporary pamphlets and are regarded by researchers as exaggerated.

serien.name: Price in years of a craftsman's income

bloecke.md:
## Trading in delivery contracts

While they were being traded, the bulbs were in the ground. What changed hands were therefore contracts for delivery in the summer. Contemporaries called this business the [[Wind trade (windhandel)|wind trade (windhandel)]]. Deals were struck in taverns and recorded on slips of paper, and payment was due only on delivery. Buyers therefore initially had to put up almost no money. This created leverage without a lender. No bank provided any money; the payment obligation itself took the lender's place.

This also explains why the collapse had almost no consequences for the wider economy. In the archives, the historian Anne Goldgar found around 285 traders in Haarlem who were demonstrably involved, about 60 in Amsterdam and about 25 in Enkhuizen. The trade therefore involved a small circle of wealthy merchants and master craftsmen and not the population at large. The Dutch economy carried on undisturbed after 1637.

Almost everything that is told about dancing crowds and ruined farmers goes back to Charles Mackay's compilation of 1841 and not to sources from 1637. If you use an anecdote about a bubble as evidence for an investment principle, you should therefore know how old it is and how well documented it is. The price fall of over 95% is also an estimate and not a measured value.

The damage also remained small because the claims were never enforced. At the beginning of February 1637, trading came to a standstill. The Court of Holland suspended enforcement and referred the matter back to the towns. In 1638, Haarlem released buyers from their contracts in return for payment of around 3.5% of the purchase price. Legally, the contracts corresponded to what is now called gaming and betting. They were binding only as long as both sides wanted to fulfil them.

On this point, the legal position today is different. Under Section 762 BGB (Civil Code), gaming and betting still do not create an enforceable obligation, but Section 99 WpHG (Securities Trading Act) expressly exempts financial futures transactions (Finanztermingeschäfte) from this rule. Buyers of a leveraged derivative therefore cannot invoke the gaming defence. The risk for private investors is limited elsewhere. In 2017, BaFin (Federal Financial Supervisory Authority) prohibited the marketing to retail clients of contracts for difference (CFDs) with an [[Obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht)|obligation to make additional payments (Nachschusspflicht)]]. With these products, the loss can therefore reach the amount invested but cannot exceed it.

## Paris 1719 and the Mississippi Company

In Paris, the Scotsman John Law founded the Banque Générale in 1716 and the Mississippi Company in 1717. From 1718, the bank operated as the Banque Royale under a state guarantee. The company's trading territory, French Louisiana, was barely developed and generated no income. The company's business consisted mainly of taking over French government debt and paying the creditors with its own shares. These shares, in turn, were bought with banknotes printed by Law's own bank.

The share price rose from 500 livres in 1717 to around 10,000 livres in December 1719, and forward contracts were at times quoted at 14,000. To keep the price from falling, the quantity of notes had to grow with it, and every new issue of notes drove prices up. In January 1720, inflation in France was running at around 23% a month (not a year). In November 1720, France abolished paper money and returned to a metallic currency. By September 1721, the share was back at 500 livres. The word *millionaire* dates from this period.

bloecke.titel: Law's cycle of banknotes and shares
bloecke.unter: Each stage financed the next, and the funds for it came from the same printing press; the rise in the share price rested on this cycle and not on any valuation of Louisiana.

bloecke.md: If the same institution issues a security and at the same time creates the money with which it is bought, the rise in its price rests on a cycle and not on a valuation.

## London 1720 and the South Sea Company

The South Sea Company had been founded in 1711 with a trading monopoly for Spanish South America. The trade itself remained very small because Spain in effect allowed only one ship a year. The business model resembled the one in Paris, but without a printing press of its own. When it was founded, the company had already taken over around £9 million of British government debt and given the creditors its own shares in return. In January 1720, it offered to take over around £31 million more in the same way, and in April 1720 Parliament agreed. This resembled a [[Debt-for-equity swap|debt-for-equity swap]] on a large scale, except that the creditors received shares in the company and not stakes in the debtor, the state.

This exchange created the incentive that explains the bubble. The higher the share price, the fewer shares the company had to hand over per pound of debt exchanged. It could sell on the remaining shares. The directors were therefore interested in a high share price and not a fair one. Accordingly, the company issued new tranches against payment in instalments and lent buyers money so that they could buy its shares. The price rose from around £128 in January to around £950 in July. After 18 August it fell from over £800 to £200 and reached its low of £124 in December.

bloecke.titel: Share prices of two bubbles in the same year, rebased to 100
bloecke.unter: Both prices are indexed to their starting value (Mississippi 500 livres, South Sea £128); the axis is logarithmic so that the English curve remains clearly visible next to the French one.

bloecke.md:
Isaac Newton was Master of the Mint and a shareholder in the South Sea Company. According to the surviving accounts, he sold at a profit in the spring of 1720, later bought back in at peak prices and lost around £20,000. His exact prices are not documented. However, the sequence can be recalculated with the documented benchmark figures:

- An investment of £1,000 at a price of 128 buys 7.81 shares.
- Selling at 300 brings in £2,343.75, a gain of around 134%.
- Buying back in with the full proceeds at 800 buys 2.93 shares.
- At the December low of 124, these shares are worth around £363.

In this way, £1,000 turns into around £363, even though a gain of around 134% had been reached in between. The loss is caused by buying back in with the larger amount at the higher price, not by holding. The well-known Newton quotation about the madness of people is not documented in contemporary sources and is regarded as a later attribution.

bloecke.md:
## Regulation then and now

In June 1720, the British Parliament passed the [[Bubble Act]], which prohibited joint-stock companies without a royal charter. The act came before the crash. It was intended to stop copycat companies that were taking money from the public that would otherwise have flowed into South Sea Company shares, and the South Sea Company itself had lobbied for it. In addition, it regulated only the legal form and not the mechanism. Loans against the company's own shares, the directors' conflict of interest and the missing cash flow remained unregulated. The act worked above all as a brake. The joint-stock company remained the exception in Britain for around a hundred years, until the Bubble Act was repealed in 1825. France reacted in a similarly sweeping and equally untargeted way by abolishing paper money as such.

German law today intervenes at three other points. A public offering requires an approved prospectus under the EU Prospectus Regulation 2017/1129 in conjunction with the WpPG (Securities Prospectus Act), and the offeror is liable for false information (Sections 9 et seq. WpPG). Market manipulation is prohibited under Article 15 of the Market Abuse Regulation (MAR) and is punishable as an administrative offence with a fine (Section 120 WpHG). It is a criminal offence under Section 119 WpHG if it is committed intentionally and thereby affects the stock exchange or market price; attempts are also punishable. The construction that supported the share price in 1720 is also expressly ruled out today. Under Section 71a(1) AktG (Stock Corporation Act), legal transactions by which a public limited company (AG) finances the acquisition of its own shares are void. These rules do not prevent a bubble. They do, however, change who is liable afterwards, and they make involvement provable.

## Three recurring mechanisms

1. There was no cash flow to back the prices. Bulbs, Louisiana and the South America trade yielded nothing that could have supported such a price. The only reference point for the valuation was the last price paid.
2. The purchases were based on credit that was not perceived as credit. With the tulips, leverage worked without a bank; in Paris, it came with a printing press; in London, it came from the issuer in favour of its own shares. In all three cases, you could buy without paying immediately.
3. The issuer had its own interest in the share price. A provider that issues securities and at the same time profits from their price is not neutral. Today this situation must be disclosed, but in its basic form it still exists.

Whether a current market shows these features can be checked without making a forecast. To do so, you need to establish where the cash flow comes from, who is financing the buyers and who holds the other side of the trade.

bloecke.titel: Tax consequences of a total loss
bloecke.md: Under Section 32d(1) EStG (Income Tax Act), capital income is subject to the 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus the solidarity surcharge and, where applicable, church tax. Before that, the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 is deducted, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG). Losses from the sale of shares may be offset only against gains from share sales (Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG). An investor who holds only one position and loses it therefore has no gain against which to offset the loss. The separate offsetting category for shares thus softens the damage least precisely when the damage is greatest.

mitnehmen: The price collapse begins when the next buyer fails to appear, and it needs no bad news to do so.

In all three episodes, credit propped up the price, in the form of delivery contracts without a down payment, note printing by the company's own bank and loans from the issuer for buying its own shares.
Getting out at a profit offers no security in itself, because the costly mistake of 1720 was buying back in later at the peak price, not holding.
Regulation in response to a bubble usually targets the legal form instead of the mechanism; Section 71a AktG is a late exception.
Three things can be checked: the cash flow, how the buyers are financed and the issuer's interests.

begriffe.text: Dutch term for trading in delivery contracts for goods that do not yet exist, in 1636/37 for tulip bulbs that were still in the ground. Payment was due only on delivery, so it was possible to speculate without capital.

British act of June 1720 that prohibited the formation of joint-stock companies without a royal charter. It slowed the spread of this legal form until its repeal in 1825, but it did not cover the mechanisms of speculation.

Exchange of debt instruments for stakes in the debtor. In 1719/20, the Mississippi Company and the South Sea Company took over government debt in exchange for their own shares; the creditors received stakes in the company and not in the debtor, the state. Today, the debt-for-equity swap is a common instrument in corporate restructurings.
Obligation to pay in additional money beyond the amount invested when a leveraged position goes into the red. BaFin prohibited it in 2017 for contracts for difference with retail clients.
